title: Continuity of a Function
notes: A function $f$ is continuous at $x = a$ if three conditions are met: (1) $f(a)$ is defined, (2) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$ exists, (3) $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$.
Intuitive idea: the graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil — no breaks, holes, or jumps.
A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point in that interval.
Types of discontinuity:
• Removable (hole): limit exists but $f(a)$ is undefined or different — can be 'fixed' by redefining $f(a)$.
• Jump discontinuity: left-hand limit $\neq$ right-hand limit — graph has a sudden jump.
• Infinite discontinuity: function approaches $\pm\infty$ — vertical asymptote.
• Non/removable: limit does not exist and cannot be fixed.
Algebraic functions are continuous everywhere in their domain.
Trigonometric functions (sin, cos) are continuous everywhere; tan, sec have discontinuities at odd multiples of $\pi/2$.
Exponential ($e^x$) and logarithmic ($\ln x$) functions are continuous on their domains.
Sum, difference, product, and quotient (where denominator $\neq 0$) of continuous functions are continuous.
Composite of continuous functions is continuous.
Formal Definition (\varepsilon-$\delta$)
$f$ is continuous at $a$ if for every $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $|f(x) - f(a)| < \varepsilon$ whenever $|x - a| < \delta$.
Left and Right Continuity
$f$ is right-continuous at $a$: $\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$.
$f$ is left-continuous at $a$: $\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = f(a)$.
$f$ is continuous at $a$ if and only if it is both left and right continuous at $a$.
Continuity on Intervals
Open interval $(a,b)$: $f$ is continuous on $(a,b)$ if it is continuous at every point in the interval.
Closed interval $[a,b]$: $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ if continuous on $(a,b)$, right-continuous at $a$, and left-continuous at $b$.
Important Theorems
Intermediate Value Theorem: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and $k$ is between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, there exists $c \in (a,b)$ such that $f(c) = k$.
Extreme Value Theorem: If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $f$ attains both a maximum and minimum value on $[a,b]$.
Continuity of composite: If $f$ is continuous at $c$ and $g$ is continuous at $f(c)$, then $g \circ f$ is continuous at $c$.
confusion: Continuity at a point requires the limit to exist — check both LHL and RHS separately.
A function can be continuous on an interval but discontinuous at a single point.
Differentiability implies continuity, but continuity does NOT imply differentiability (e.g., $|x|$ at $x=0$).
A function being defined at a point does NOT make it continuous there — the limit must match the function value.
Piecewise functions require checking continuity at the boundary points carefully by computing LHL, RHS, and the function value.
Removable discontinuities can be 'removed' by redefining the function at a single point, while essential discontinuities cannot be fixed.
practice: Find the value of $k$ that makes $f(x)$ continuous at $x = 2$, where $f(x) = \frac{x^2-4}{x-2}$ for $x \neq 2$ and $f(2) = k$.
Show that $f(x) = [x]$ (greatest integer function) is discontinuous at every integer.
Determine the continuity of $f(x) = \frac{\sin x}{x}$ at $x = 0$.
If $f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2+1 & x < 2 \\ kx & x \geq 2 \end{cases}$ is continuous at $x=2$, find $k$.
universalFacts: Continuity is a prerequisite for differentiability — you cannot differentiate a function at a point where it is discontinuous.
The Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees that a continuous function on $[a,b]$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
Physical quantities that change continuously (position, temperature) can be modeled with continuous functions.
A continuous function on a closed interval is uniformly continuous (Heine-Cantor theorem).
The set of points where a function is continuous is always a $G_\delta$ set (countable intersection of open sets).
